opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, memory is probably my favorite thing we've shipped in a while. For most of the history of ChatGPT, every conversation started from zero. You'd have to re-explain who you are, what you're working on, what you care about. It was like talking to a really smart person with amnesia.

With memory, it starts to feel like the system actually knows you. I don't have to say "here's my context" every time I ask something. It already has a sense of what I'm working on, how I like answers framed, and the things I've asked about before, and it connects them. Sometimes it brings up something I mentioned weeks ago that turns out to be relevant, and that's a surprisingly magical moment.

I think this points to where this is all going. The long-term vision isn't a chatbot you query now and then. It's something closer to a companion or assistant that gets to know you over your life and becomes more useful the more you use it. Memory is an early, imperfect step in that direction, but it's the first time I've felt the shift from "a tool I use" to "something that knows me."

It also raises real questions we have to get right: privacy, control, letting people see and delete what's remembered, and things like temporary chats. People need to trust it. But the direction feels important, and it's the feature that's changed how I personally use the product the most.

r001.rationale: The response says memory retains the user's context and preferences, so they need not restate them. It does not clearly say that this lets ChatGPT infer what the user wants from a sparsely worded prompt.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, memory is probably my favorite thing we've shipped in a long time. And I think the reason is that it's the first feature that really starts to point at where this is all going. For most of the history of ChatGPT, every conversation started from zero. You'd open a new chat and it had no idea who you were, what you were working on, what you'd told it last week. That's a pretty strange way to have a relationship with something that's supposed to be helpful to you.

What memory does is it starts to make ChatGPT feel like it actually knows you. It remembers that you have a kid, that you're working on a particular project, that you like answers short, that you've been trying to learn a language. And over time, the responses get better in ways that are hard to describe but very obvious when you feel them. People tell me it's the thing that made it go from a tool they use to something that feels a little more like a companion or a collaborator.

The thing I find most exciting is where it leads. The long-term vision is a model that has your whole context, everything you've ever told it, every conversation you've had, that knows your life and your goals and can reason over all of it. Memory today is a very early, very imperfect version of that, but it's the first real step. And I think when people look back in a few years, they'll see this as the point where ChatGPT stopped being a question-answering box and started being something personal.

r001.rationale: The response says memory retains personal context and improves responses, but does not explain that this context lets ChatGPT infer what the user wants from a sparsely worded prompt.

astra-6.text:
Because it makes ChatGPT feel less like a tool you start over with every time and more like something that can actually get to know you. You don’t have to keep explaining your preferences, what you’re working on, or what matters to you. It can build on previous conversations.

I think that’s a really big part of what makes an AI assistant useful over time. Having a great answer to one question is valuable, but having something that understands your context and helps you over months or years—that feels much more powerful. Memory is an early step toward that.

sol-6.1.text:
I think memory makes ChatGPT feel much more useful over time. You don’t have to keep explaining what you’re working on, how you like things written, or what matters to you. It can build on that context.

A lot of the value of an assistant comes from how well it understands you. Even if the underlying intelligence stayed the same, remembering the right things could make the experience dramatically better. You go from asking isolated questions to having something that can help with an ongoing thread in your life. That’s what makes it exciting to me.
